issues.description: The manuscript’s central claim that causal understanding is not necessary is stronger than what the experiment can establish. The study measures only a narrow form of explicit post-task understanding, not all forms of causal understanding, tacit knowledge, heuristics, or implicit physical intuitions. Demonstrating that measured explicit understanding did not increase does not prove that causal understanding was absent or unnecessary for participants’ search behavior.
issues.quote: Causal understanding is not necessary for the improvement of culturally evolving technology

issues.description: The discussion acknowledges that participants used appropriate intuitions to restrict exploration. These intuitions may themselves constitute implicit causal understanding or learned physical knowledge. This directly weakens the interpretation that optimization occurred in the absence of causal understanding.
issues.quote: This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard.

issues.description: The study lacks a no-transmission/asocial control condition, such as independent participants completing the same number of cumulative trials without inherited configurations, or single individuals completing 25 trials. Without such a control, it is difficult to isolate the contribution of cultural transmission and selective retention from individual learning, general task affordances, regression to good configurations, or other experimental dynamics.
issues.quote: Participants were organized into chains of 5 individuals. Each participant had 5 trials to minimize the time it took for the wheel to reach the end of the track.

issues.description: Understanding was measured only after the building task. Without a pre-task measure, the study cannot determine whether individuals learned during the task, whether generations differed at baseline, or whether participants entered with pre-existing understanding. The absence of a generational trend in post-task scores is not equivalent to absence of learning or absence of causal understanding.
issues.quote: participants’ understanding of how the device worked at each generation

issues.description: Because understanding was assessed only after participants had completed their five trials and after exposure to inherited information, the test conflates prior understanding, learning from personal exploration, learning from social information, and possible memory of observed outcomes.
issues.quote: Participants’ understanding was evaluated after they completed their 5 trials by asking them to predict which of two wheels would cover the distance faster

issues.subcategory: limited construct validity of understanding test
issues.description: The test uses only 10 pairwise judgments, split into 5 inertia and 5 centre-of-mass items. This is a very limited and unvalidated measure of causal understanding. It may fail to detect partial, implicit, procedural, probabilistic, or verbal causal knowledge, and its low item count likely produces substantial measurement error.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.description: Participants were asked only to choose which wheel was faster or indicate no difference, not to explain mechanisms or estimate quantitative effects. This limits the ability to infer causal understanding from the score and may misclassify participants who have qualitative but not comparative understanding, or who understand one principle but not item-specific magnitudes.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: “Wheel 1”, “Wheel 2” or “No difference”.

issues.description: All participants received the same understanding-test items in the same order. This allows item order, fatigue, learning during the test, response bias, or principle-order confounds to affect scores. Without counterbalancing, differences between inertia and centre-of-mass scores may partly reflect order effects.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.subcategory: weak manipulation of causal theory transmission
issues.description: The 'theory' manipulation is a short written sentence stem focused on what makes the wheel faster. This may elicit rules of thumb or recipes rather than causal models. The severe character limit and forced wording constrain expression of multidimensional causal explanations, making broad conclusions about transmission of causal models unwarranted.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with “The wheel covers the distance faster when...”.

issues.description: The timing of theory writing relative to the understanding test is unclear. If theories were written after or during the test phase, the test itself could influence the theory. If theories were written before the test, that should be stated explicitly. This ambiguity affects replicability and interpretation of theory coding.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to write their theory before the test phase was completed.

issues.description: Participants in the Configurations + Theory treatment were not only exposed to inherited theories; they were also told they could write and receive theories. This may change attention, motivation, explicit hypothesis generation, or exploration independently of receiving a prior theory. Therefore, treatment differences cannot be attributed solely to inherited causal information.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment, participants were also informed that they could write/receive a theory.

issues.description: The conclusion that transmitting causal models has no noticeable effect is too broad for a manipulation consisting of one short written statement from the previous participant. Human causal-model transmission often involves teaching, demonstration, dialogue, diagrams, cumulative revision, and feedback. The null effect of this restricted manipulation does not justify general claims about causal model transmission.
issues.quote: we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution

issues.description: The analyses comparing participants who inherited inertia, centre-of-mass, full, or irrelevant theories are observational. Participants were not randomly assigned to inherit theory types. Theory type is likely confounded with the predecessor’s configurations, performance, search behavior, chain history, and generation. Causal statements that inherited theories affected exploration or understanding are therefore not justified.
issues.quote: Participants who inherited an inertia theory mainly produced compact and balanced wheels

issues.subcategory: theory content confounded with transmitted configurations
issues.description: In the theory treatment, participants inherited both configurations and theories from the same previous participant. Thus, differences attributed to inherited theories may instead be caused by the inherited configurations and their scores, or by consistency between configurations and theory. The design does not isolate the independent effect of theory content.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system.

issues.subcategory: exploratory subgroup analyses with small cells
issues.description: The exploratory theory-type analyses rely on small and uneven groups, including only six participants inheriting a full theory. Such small subgroups produce unstable estimates and make visual differences in heat maps and understanding scores difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: The few participants who inherited a full theory produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (Figure 3D and H).

issues.description: The manuscript presents exploratory subgroup patterns as strong evidence that theories constrained exploration and understanding. Without preregistered tests, appropriate uncertainty estimates, correction for multiple comparisons, or random assignment of theory content, these findings should be framed much more cautiously.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants’ exploration behavior

issues.description: The manuscript infers that exploration patterns caused later understanding patterns, but participants with different prior intuitions or understanding may have chosen different exploration strategies in the first place. Because exploration type was not randomized, the direction of causality cannot be established.
issues.quote: These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.subcategory: null effects interpreted without equivalence testing
issues.description: The manuscript interprets intervals overlapping zero as evidence of no effect or no substantial support. However, no equivalence bounds, ROPE, Bayes factors, or decision criteria are provided. The reported intervals are wide and include effects that may be practically meaningful.
issues.quote: Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h

issues.description: For understanding, the Generation x Treatment interval is reported as excluding zero, yet the text states that analyses do not provide substantial support for an effect of theory transmission on understanding. The manuscript should report model-predicted contrasts and clarify whether the interaction is considered evidence of differential change.
issues.quote: Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44

issues.description: The study did not use statistical methods to determine sample size. With only 14 chains per treatment, the experiment may be underpowered for treatment differences, interactions, sex effects, and understanding outcomes. Referring to previous publications does not establish adequate power for the present hypotheses.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications30,31.

issues.description: The effective independent unit for cultural transmission is the chain, not the individual trial or participant. With 14 chains per treatment and serial dependence within chains, estimates of generation and treatment effects are fragile. Random intercepts may not adequately capture inheritance-based autocorrelation or chain-specific trajectories.
issues.quote: Each treatment involved 14 chains each containing 5 individuals.

issues.description: Configurations and scores are transmitted down chains, so observations are causally and temporally dependent. The reported models include random effects but do not appear to model autoregressive dependence, inherited starting point, predecessor performance, or chain-specific slopes, which may underestimate uncertainty or misattribute effects to generation.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable, “Trial”, “Generation” as predictor variables and “Player’s identity” and “Chain’s identity” as random effects

issues.description: The performance plots average speed only for wheels that descended, while failures are shown separately. If failures differ across generation or treatment, excluding them from speed averages biases estimates of performance improvement. Failures are part of technological performance and should be modeled directly or assigned an appropriate performance value.
issues.quote: Coloured lines show the average speed for non-failure wheels at each trial in each treatment.

issues.description: The preregistered speed analyses use only participants’ last two trials to reduce failures. This changes the estimand from overall performance or learning trajectory to selected late performance and can inflate apparent optimization. It also discards information about exploration and early failures that may differ by treatment.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.description: The manuscript says no data points were excluded, but the main speed analyses were restricted to last two trials and the plotted averages exclude failure wheels. This is at least a reporting ambiguity and may be misleading about the analyzed dataset.
issues.quote: No data points were excluded from the analyses.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate linear model for bounded/count outcomes
issues.description: Wheel speed is bounded and affected by failures; understanding scores are discrete counts from a small number of items. Linear Gaussian models may produce inappropriate uncertainty and predictions. Item-level binomial/multinomial models for understanding and models accommodating censoring/failures or bounded speed would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Score” as the outcome variable, “Generation” as a predictor variable and “Chain’s identity” as a random effect

issues.description: The final model was selected by comparing candidate models based on fit to observed data. If not preregistered and if model uncertainty is ignored, this can inflate confidence and bias inference. The criteria for selection are not described in the main text.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.description: The preregistered understanding analysis was changed after observing a negative correlation and convergence problems. Aggregating across physical principles removes theoretically important variation and can mask opposite effects on inertia and centre-of-mass understanding. Alternative item-level or multivariate models could have addressed the convergence issue without changing the estimand.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.description: The manuscript states that Bayesian multilevel models were used but does not report priors, convergence diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, effective sample sizes, or model fit criteria in the main methods. These are necessary for evaluating Bayesian inferences and replicability.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32.  Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently refers to confidence intervals, credible intervals, and highest posterior density intervals. In a Bayesian analysis, these quantities have different meanings from frequentist confidence intervals. Ambiguous terminology can mislead readers about the inferential framework.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding with manual apparatus operation
issues.description: The experimenter manually positioned the weights and operated the physical apparatus, while data collection was not blind to treatment. Even if timing was automated, subtle differences in placement, release, or handling could influence wheel performance, especially when effects are modest.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.description: Each configuration appears to have been run once, with no repeated measurements or report of timing precision, release reliability, friction variability, or calibration. Measurement noise could affect displayed scores and therefore be culturally transmitted as if it reflected real design differences.
issues.quote: Once released, the time it took the wheel to descend the track was automatically recorded by the computer program.

issues.description: The manuscript describes the track as 1 meter and says speed was calculated as 1m/descent time, but the methods state that timing switches were 92 cm apart. This discrepancy affects reported speeds, maximum speed, payoffs, and replicability.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time)

issues.description: The actual recorded distance appears to be 92 cm rather than 1 meter. The manuscript should clarify whether speed was calculated over 92 cm, 1 m, or another distance, and whether all reported speeds and payoffs use the same value.
issues.quote: Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails and connected to a computer program

issues.subcategory: unclear maximum speed and optimization calculation
issues.description: The maximum possible speed is reported as about 154 m/h, whereas the payoff formula uses MaxSpeed = 160. The derivation of the maximum and the calculation of '71% optimization' are not sufficiently explained, making the optimization claim difficult to verify.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.description: The main models treat generation as a linear predictor across only five generations. Cultural accumulation may be nonlinear, with rapid early gains and later saturation near the maximum speed. A linear coefficient may misrepresent the trajectory and obscure treatment differences.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable, “Trial”, “Generation” as predictor variables

issues.description: The manuscript says that assignment and organization were randomized, but it does not describe the randomization procedure, blocking, temporal ordering, or allocation by sex and treatment. In sequential chain experiments, inadequate randomization can introduce batch, order, experimenter, or cohort confounds.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one condition of the experiment and one sex-segregated chain.

issues.description: All chains were exclusively male or exclusively female, but the manuscript does not report treatment balance by sex, model sex effects, or examine whether chain sex composition affected transmission. This limits generalization to mixed-gender social learning contexts.
issues.quote: participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females).

issues.description: The discussion explicitly claims generalization beyond single-sex chain compositions to mixed-gender collaborative settings, but the experiment did not include mixed-gender chains or collaborative interaction. This conclusion is unsupported by the design.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.description: The sample consists of French university students, a narrow and highly educated population. Claims about human technological evolution, ancestral cognition, and traditional technologies may not generalize from this population, especially given possible effects of formal education and culturally learned physical intuitions.
issues.quote: French university students

issues.description: The manuscript states that the cultural niche hypothesis predicts no improvement in understanding. The hypothesis that cumulative culture can occur without complete causal understanding does not necessarily predict that understanding will not improve, nor that causal reasoning plays no role. This risks setting up an overly strong contrast between cultural accumulation and causal cognition.
issues.quote: The cultural niche hypothesis predicts that the speed of the wheel will increase with generations, while participants’ understanding of the system will not improve over generations

issues.description: The task is a simplified, low-dimensional laboratory optimization problem with discrete positions and immediate feedback. Results from this system may not generalize to real technologies involving many dimensions, materials, social collaboration, long learning times, and richer causal reasoning.
issues.quote: the optimization problem is low-dimensional

issues.description: The manuscript claims the task has ecological validity because performance depends on physics rather than arbitrary principles. However, the apparatus, discrete sliders, short-term feedback, and laboratory reward structure are artificial and may not capture ecological features of technological production.
issues.quote: the performance of the wheel depends solely on the laws of physics, and not on arbitrary principles that could compromise the ecological validity of our results

issues.subcategory: real apparatus depends on unmodeled factors
issues.description: The manuscript states that performance depends on only moment of inertia and centre of mass, but the physical apparatus may also be affected by friction, slipping, alignment, release variability, spoke/weight tolerances, and measurement noise. Treating performance as dependent on only two variables may overstate the precision of causal-understanding assessment.
issues.quote: The time required for the wheel to cover the track depends on just two variables: its moment of inertia and the position of its centre of mass

issues.subcategory: unclear handling of failures in payoff and models
issues.description: The manuscript shows failures and says the bonus is zero for non-descending wheels, but it does not clearly state how recorded speed or payoff was computed for failures in all analyses. Because failures are common enough to plot, their treatment is important for interpreting performance.
issues.quote: Bonus took the value 0.2 for wheels that descended and 0 otherwise.

issues.subcategory: no direct modeling of failure probability
issues.description: Failures are an important binary performance outcome but are not modeled as an outcome. A treatment or generation could improve average speed among successful wheels while worsening failure probability, or vice versa. Ignoring this joint outcome can distort conclusions about optimization.
issues.quote: Vertical bars show the number of wheels that did not descend (i.e. failures) at each trial in each treatment.

issues.description: The manuscript reports equal numbers of men and women overall but does not specify how many male and female chains were assigned to each treatment. If sex composition differed by treatment or generation order, it could confound treatment effects.
issues.quote: In total, 140 participants took part in the study (70 women and 70 men).

issues.description: Participants’ physics or engineering background was measured but is not included in the main models. Even if supplementary analyses found no effect, the manuscript does not report how many participants had such backgrounds or whether background was balanced across treatments, generations, and chains.
issues.quote: At the end of the experiment, participants indicated whether they have an academic background in physics or engineering.

issues.description: The theory-coding scheme classifies theories only by whether they contain accurate inertia and/or centre-of-mass information. Incorrect, partially correct, mechanistic, procedural, or misleading theories may differ substantially in their effects but are collapsed into broad categories such as irrelevant.
issues.quote: asked to code participants’ theories according to whether they contain accurate information related to moment of inertia and/or centre of mass

issues.subcategory: inappropriate or unclear interrater reliability statistic
issues.description: Three coders rated the theories, but the manuscript reports Cohen’s kappa, which is conventionally a two-rater statistic unless pairwise kappas or an extension is used. The manuscript does not explain how kappa was computed for three raters or how disagreements were resolved.
issues.quote: 3 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel

issues.description: Although interrater reliability is reported, the final coding procedure is not described. It is unclear whether disagreements were resolved by majority vote, discussion, one primary coder, or another rule, which affects reproducibility of the theory-category analyses.
issues.quote: Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.subcategory: theories may transmit recipes rather than causal explanations
issues.description: The manuscript says participants could not transmit performance information about specific configurations, but the examples of centre-of-mass theories are close to design recipes indicating where to place weights. This means the theory condition may add extra configuration information rather than purely causal understanding.
issues.quote: Participants could not transmit information about the performance of a specific configuration in order to prevent individuals from extending the number of transmitted configurations as compared to the “Configurations” treatment.

issues.subcategory: no enforcement described for theory-content restriction
issues.description: The manuscript does not describe whether transmitted theories were screened or edited to prevent participants from including specific configuration-performance information. If participants could include such information, the Configurations + Theory condition is not cleanly comparable to the Configurations condition.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with “The wheel covers the distance faster when...”.

issues.subcategory: incentive structure may alter exploration and transmission
issues.description: Participants were paid based partly on the next participant’s performance. This may induce strategic behavior, such as using final trials to communicate, demonstrate, or preserve interpretable configurations, rather than simply optimizing individual performance. The incentive also creates dependence across participants beyond social-information transmission.
issues.quote: their reward depended both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in the chain

issues.subcategory: unequal actual payoff rule for final generation
issues.description: Final participants did not have a next participant, and their last two payoffs were doubled without their knowledge. Although participants did not know chain position, this means the actual payoff function differed by generation, which should be considered when interpreting behavior and incentives.
issues.quote: Final participants in chains had their last two payoffs doubled (although they were not aware of this as they didn’t know that the chain was about to end).

issues.subcategory: unclear score scale and chance level
issues.description: Understanding scores are reported without clearly defining whether the score is out of 10 overall or out of 5 by principle in each analysis, how 'No difference' responses were scored, and what exact chance level was used. This makes interpretation of values such as 4.60 and comparisons to chance less transparent.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h (95% Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6)) and their understanding score was 4.60

issues.description: The manuscript states that some groups scored better than chance, but it does not report formal statistical tests or credible intervals for comparisons to chance, especially for principle-specific scores and small inherited-theory subgroups.
issues.quote: Participants who did not inherit any theory (“Configurations” treatment) scored similarly (and better than chance) on questions about inertia and questions about centre of mass

issues.subcategory: ambiguous treatment of first-generation theory participants
issues.description: First-generation participants in the theory condition could not inherit theories but were instructed differently and wrote theories. It is unclear how they are handled in some comparisons of participants who did or did not inherit theories, which can affect treatment and subgroup interpretations.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory (all participants in the “Configurations + Theory” treatment except first-generation participants)

issues.description: The manuscript argues that better understanding of one dimension and worse understanding of another compensate in the aggregate. This illustrates why the aggregated score is problematic: total scores can appear unchanged even when theory transmission changes the structure of understanding in theoretically important ways.
issues.quote: with our 2-dimensional problem, better understanding of one dimension and worse understanding of one dimension simply compensate each other

issues.description: Several important methodological and analytical details are deferred to supplementary figures, tables, methods, code, and OSF materials. While data/code availability is valuable, the main manuscript should contain enough detail to evaluate core claims without relying on external files.
issues.quote: see Supplementary Table 1 for model output
